new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. Tone There appear to be only two tone levels lexically-High and Low; Mid tone and Falling tone occur grammatically. Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted. 2b. Stress Stress, sometimes accompanied by a slight degree of length, seems to fall on the first syllable of a word Stem. The Noun Class Suffix is never stressed.
new_statements.citation: Tucker, A. N. & M. A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa (Handbook of African Languages). London: Oxford University Press for the International African Institute.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 4 'The Mba (Class) Languages' (chapter opens p. 108: 'The four languages of this Group, MBA ('Kimanga'), NDUNGA ('Mondunga'), 'DONGO, and MA ('Amadi')'), sec. 2 'Tone and Stress', 2b 'Stress', p. 109 (page from chapter-opening snippet '( 108)', archive.org scandata leaf 121 = p. 109, Google Books reprint PT115).
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Mba-group languages (Mba, Ndunga, Dongo, Ma) stress, often with slight lengthening, falls on the first syllable of the word stem; the noun-class suffix (these languages mark class by suffix) is never stressed. Lexical tone has two levels (H, L). Stated tentatively ('seems to') for the group as a whole from Tucker & Hackett's field notes, not for Ma individually.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that the noun-class suffix is never stressed; no other exceptions in the snippets seen. Ma nouns carry an initial vowel a-/U- (prefix-like element) per the same chapter, so stem-initial stress is not necessarily word-initial in Ma.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level impressionistic statement in a comparative handbook chapter; tonal language (2 lexical levels) with a stress remark; hedged ('seems to'); applies to the four-language group, Ma included by name in the chapter scope. Full page not seen (controlled-lending scan); text assembled from overlapping verbatim scanned search snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress statement is a GROUP-LEVEL generalisation in Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 4 'The Mba (Class) Languages', which explicitly covers four languages: MBA ('Kimanga', mbaa1245), NDUNGA ('Mondunga', ndun1249), 'DONGO (dong1293?) and MA ('Amadi') = made1252, with Ma variants named Amadi, Dakwa and Niangara; data from A. N. Tucker & P. E. Hackett field notes (LSNBB). It is not stated for Ma separately. The same sentence was used by the sibling audit for mbaa1245. Czekanowski's 'Madyo' (wordlist, Gumbari soldiers) is equated with Ma by Tucker & Bryan 1956 ('MA (AMADI, MADI, MADYO &c.), own name (a)ma-lo').
